lead: A laser does not work by making atoms emit more often. It works by arranging more atoms in an upper energy level than in a lower one. That arrangement is population inversion. A pump supplies energy to create it, and two mirrors keep light passing through the gain medium many times. This chapter explains inversion, pumping, the threshold for laser action, and the four standard laser characteristics: monochromaticity, coherence, directionality and brightness. These ideas explain why a laser pointer is so different from a torch, and they set up the named lasers in 5.3–5.5.
prereq: You need: Einstein coefficients from 5.1 and the Boltzmann factor from Unit 6.

sections.h3: Thermal equilibrium gives absorption, not gain

blocks.text: Take two energy levels: lower level 1 with population N₁ and upper level 2 with population N₂. Population means number of atoms per unit volume. At thermal equilibrium the Boltzmann factor gives

blocks.where: g₂ and g₁ are degeneracies; ΔE = E₂ − E₁ is the transition energy in joules; k_B is Boltzmann's constant; T is absolute temperature in kelvin.

blocks.text: For equal degeneracies g₂ = g₁ = 1, the ratio is exp(−ΔE/(k_B T)). Visible photons have ΔE much larger than k_B T at room temperature, so N₂ is far smaller than N₁.

Light in the medium causes absorption 1→2 and stimulated emission 2→1. The rates are B₁₂N₁ρ and B₂₁N₂ρ, where ρ is the energy density of the radiation; B₁₂ and B₂₁ are equal only when g₁ = g₂. Absorption wins when N₁ > N₂. Net amplification needs N₂ > N₁. This is population inversion. It is a non-equilibrium state: the upper level holds more atoms than the lower one. With unequal degeneracies the condition is N₂/g₂ > N₁/g₁; the simple form N₂ > N₁ assumes equal degeneracies.

An ordinary excited atom returns by spontaneous emission in nanoseconds, too fast to store atoms. A laser uses a metastable level: an excited level with a long spontaneous lifetime, often milliseconds. Atoms collect there while the pump supplies energy. The metastable level is the upper laser level.

Pumping moves atoms from lower levels to the upper level. Common methods are optical pumping (a flashlamp or another laser supplies photons), electrical pumping (a gas discharge or forward-biased semiconductor junction supplies energetic electrons), and chemical pumping (a reaction produces excited molecules). The pump must maintain N₂ > N₁; it need not be light.

In a three-level scheme the lower laser level is the ground state. More than half the atoms must leave the ground state before inversion begins, so threshold pump power is high. Ruby is the standard example; see 5.3. In a four-level scheme the lower laser level sits above the ground state and empties quickly. Inversion starts when a few atoms reach the upper level, so threshold is much lower. Nd:YAG is a common four-level laser; see 5.4.

The gain medium sits between two mirrors: M₁ is highly reflecting, M₂ is partially reflecting. Together they form an optical cavity or resonator. Light along the cavity axis passes through the medium many times. Each pass adds photons by stimulated emission. The partial mirror lets a small fraction leave as the output beam.

blocks.where: R₁, R₂ are mirror reflectances (0 to 1); g is gain coefficient per metre; α is loss coefficient per metre; L is gain-medium length in metres.

blocks.text: The left side is the fraction of light surviving one round trip. Below 1, light dies out. Above threshold, output grows until gain saturation limits it. Some syllabi call this the round-trip gain condition.

Continuous-wave (CW) operation gives steady output. Pulsed operation stores energy and releases it in short bursts. CW lasers need cooling because the pump heats the medium; pulsed lasers reach higher peak power.
Four standard characteristics separate laser light from lamp light.

items: Monochromaticity: the output occupies a narrow wavelength band Δλ around a central wavelength λ. Small Δλ/λ means a well-defined colour or frequency. No laser is perfectly single-wavelength; Δλ is small but nonzero.

Coherence: the wave keeps a fixed phase relation across the beam (spatial coherence) and along the beam for a coherence time (temporal coherence). This enables interference and holography; see Unit 4, Wave Optics.
Directionality: the beam spreads by a small divergence angle θ, so it stays narrow over long distances. A torch spreads light over a wide cone; a laser does not.
Brightness: power per unit area per unit solid angle. A laser can be bright at modest power because its beam is narrow in angle and area.

blocks.where: B_r is brightness; P is power in watts; A is beam area in square metres; Ω is solid angle in steradians.

blocks.text: The four properties are separate, but brightness is not independent of the others: a beam that is narrow in area and divergence, and carries enough power, is bright.

figure.caption: The pump raises atoms until the gain medium has N₂ > N₁. The two mirrors return light through the medium; mirror M₂ is partly transmitting, so a small output beam leaves it.

spec.title: Population inversion in a laser cavity

examples.question: For a transition of energy 1.96 eV at T = 300 K, find the thermal-equilibrium ratio N₂/N₁ for equal degeneracies. Compare it with an inverted ratio N₂/N₁ = 2. Use k_B = 8.617×10⁻⁵ eV/K.
steps: The inverted ratio N₂/N₁ = 2 is many orders of magnitude larger than the thermal-equilibrium value.
examples.answer: At 300 K, N₂/N₁ ≈ 1.2×10⁻³³, so an inverted ratio of 2 cannot occur thermally; pumping is needed.
examples.check:
import math
k = 8.617e-5
T = 300.0
dE = 1.96
kT = k * T
ratio = math.exp(-dE / kT)
print(f'{kT:.6f}')
print(f'{ratio:.1e}')
print(f'{2.0:.1f}')

traps: A bigger pump does not always give laser output. Fast non-radiative decay or a short upper-level lifetime keeps N₂ below N₁, so inversion is never reached; and even with inversion, high cavity loss or low mirror reflectance can keep the round-trip factor below 1, so oscillation never starts.
Three-level lasers are not easier because they have fewer levels; they need more than half the atoms pumped, so their threshold is higher.
N₂ > N₁ is the equal-degeneracy form. With degeneracies g₁ and g₂, use N₂/g₂ > N₁/g₁.
Thermal equilibrium never gives inversion. Heating a medium increases both populations; it does not reverse the Boltzmann ratio.
Do not confuse brightness with power. A low-power laser with a narrow beam can be brighter than a high-power lamp.

quiz.q: Define population inversion in a two-level system with equal degeneracies.
quiz.a: N₂ > N₁, where N₂ and N₁ are number densities in the upper and lower levels.

quiz.q: Why does a laser need a metastable upper level?
quiz.a: Its long spontaneous lifetime lets atoms accumulate in the upper level, so pumping can build N₂ > N₁ before they decay.

quiz.q: At T = 300 K, find k_B T in eV using k_B = 8.617×10⁻⁵ eV/K.
A cavity has R₁ = 0.99, R₂ = 0.95, g = 2.0 m⁻¹, α = 1.0 m⁻¹, L = 0.10 m. Compute the round-trip factor R₁R₂ exp[2(g − α)L] and state whether threshold is reached.
quiz.a: R₁R₂ = 0.9405; 2(g − α)L = 0.20; exp(0.20) = 1.2214; factor = 1.149. It is > 1, so threshold is reached.

quiz.q: Why does a three-level laser need a higher pump than a four-level laser?
quiz.a: Its lower laser level is the ground state, so more than half the atoms must be moved out before N₂ > N₁. A four-level lower level is empty and empties quickly, so inversion begins at low pump.
Monochromaticity means a narrow wavelength band Δλ. Coherence means a fixed phase relation across and along the beam.

quiz.q: A laser has high power but large divergence. Is its brightness necessarily high?
quiz.a: No. Brightness is power per unit area per unit solid angle; large divergence means large solid angle, so brightness falls.

beyond: Not for the exam. Diode-pumped solid-state and fibre lasers use the same inversion and cavity ideas; a fibre Bragg grating can act as a mirror. Q-switching and mode locking produce nanosecond and femtosecond pulses by controlling cavity loss and phase. High-power designs are limited by gain saturation, thermal lensing and mirror damage. Laser safety and linewidth measurement are standard laboratory topics. Search next: gain saturation, Q-switching, mode locking, fibre Bragg grating.
